title: Iqbal's Complaint
hookLine: Iqbal's poem of complaint to Allah and its answer
tomorrow: how do you teach a whole village with a poem?

cards: Every big disappointment starts a version in your head: the message you'll never send, the speech you give in the shower. Muhammad Iqbal, the poet of South Asia, sent his.

He wrote a poem in Urdu called Shikwa, the Complaint, and in it the Muslims speak straight to God: we carried your name across the world, so why do we struggle while others thrive? It's bold, and it stirred objections.
So, can you complain to God and still be faithful?

teach.b: Iqbal didn't stop there. He wrote a second poem, Jawab-e-Shikwa, the Answer to the Complaint, and in it God replies.

teach.h: KEPT THE NAME, LOST THE SPIRIT.
teach.b: The answer is tender and tough at once: the fault isn't on God's side; the people kept the name and lost the spirit. It ends with a promise, roughly: be faithful to Muhammad, and we are yours. The pairing is the point.
The complaint is brought to God, not away from him, and it's allowed to wait for an answer.

teach.h: JACOB: MY GRIEF TO GOD ALONE.
teach.b: The Qur'an has a model: Jacob, grieving his lost son, says he complains of his sorrow to God alone.

teach.h: A WEEK OF POETS AND TRAVELERS.
teach.b: Now the week, back in one breath. Al-Biruni: as they are. Usama: a human view of war.
The Burdah: the poem of the cloak. Hafiz: the tongue of the unseen. Sa'di: a garden of tales.
And today: a complaint, and an answer.

how: Iqbal's Shikwa and Jawab-e-Shikwa are recited and sung in Urdu-speaking homes, schools and gatherings, usually together, so the complaint is heard with its answer.

o: Iqbal's Urdu poem bringing a grievance straight to God
a court case in which a poet sued the king of Delhi
a list of sins read aloud on the Day of Judgment

games.q: the complaint and its answer — tap the pairs.
p: God's answer, in a second poem
kept the name, lost the spirit
took his grief to God alone

s: Iqbal left his complaint to God unanswered
he wrote a second poem, the Answer, in which God replies.
in the Answer, God says the fault lies with heaven, not the people
the answer turns it back: they kept the name and lost the spirit.
Iqbal wrote both poems in Urdu
Shikwa and Jawab-e-Shikwa, the complaint and its answer.

games.q: Dadi's knee surgery went badly. at dinner she says, quietly: i told Allah tonight, this is too much. your cousin looks shocked. what fits this week?
o: she should take it back; faith means never questioning.
honest grief brought to God sits inside faith, like Jacob's.
it shows her faith is slipping; better to change the subject.
games.why: Jacob took his sorrow to God alone, and Iqbal's complaint was spoken to God and answered. bringing it to God is still turning toward him.

practice: Take a pen and write one honest line about what disappointed you this week, the real version, not the polite one. If you pray, address it to God, as Iqbal did; otherwise, address it to the day itself.
Then leave a little space under it, for whatever answer comes.

wordCard.voice: Iqbal's Complaint: Shikwa, his Urdu poem speaking to God with a grievance, answered by his second poem, Jawab-e-Shikwa.

orig.note: Urdu (from Arabic): shikwa, a complaint; the name of Iqbal's poem.

carryVoice: The week's last line: a complaint, and an answer, both spoken to God. Seven lines gathered, one poet left.

sources.ref: Muhammad Iqbal, Jawab-e-Shikwa (the Answer to the Complaint), including its closing couplet on faithfulness to Muhammad
Qur'an 12:86 (Jacob: I complain of my grief and sorrow only to God)
